title: The Untold Story of Obadiah
paragraphs:
The Untold Story of Obadiah
The Prophet Who Stood Between Two Kingdoms While His Soul Trembled Before God
There are names in Scripture that thunder.
Moses. David. Elijah. Paul.
And then there are names that almost disappear into the dust of forgotten pages.
Names most believers skip. Names buried between wars, judgments, and genealogies. Names preached less than once every few years.
Obadiah is one of those names.
Only twenty-one verses.
One chapter.
A prophet with no recorded miracles. No famous sermons. No dramatic biography. No ark. No lions’ den. No giant slain. No prison chains broken.
Yet hidden inside this shortest book of the Old Testament is one of the fiercest warnings God ever spoke against pride, betrayal, hidden hatred, spiritual arrogance, and silent cruelty.
And maybe that is exactly why so many people avoid Obadiah.
Because Obadiah is not merely a prophecy against a nation.
It is a mirror.
A terrifying mirror.
The Book of Obadiah exposes something most people never admit publicly:
sometimes people do not destroy others with swords.
Sometimes they destroy them by watching them suffer while doing nothing.
And suddenly this ancient prophet stops feeling ancient.
Because entire friendships have died that way. Families have fractured that way. Churches have collapsed that way. Believers have backslidden that way.
People standing nearby. Watching destruction happen. Saying nothing. Doing nothing. Feeling secretly satisfied.
That is the world Obadiah walked into.
And if we are honest...
it is still our world.
The Hebrew name עֹבַדְיָה (‘Ovadyah) means:
“Servant of Yahweh.”
Not celebrity. Not influencer. Not spiritual superstar.
Servant.
That alone already confronts modern Christianity.
Because heaven remembers servants the world forgets.

Very little is known about Obadiah himself. Scholars debate the exact timeline of his ministry, though many place the prophecy shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon around 586 BC. The target of the prophecy was Edom — descendants of Esau.
And that is where the story becomes emotionally devastating.
Because Edom and Israel were not strangers.
They were family.
Jacob and Esau.
Brothers.
The wound began in Genesis.
Two nations struggling inside one womb.
Genesis 25:23 records the Hebrew:
“וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר”
“ve-rav ya’avod tsa’ir”
“The older shall serve the younger.”
From the very beginning there was tension. Competition. Jealousy. Bitterness. Inheritance conflict.
The kind of emotional poison that silently travels through generations.
And centuries later, Edom still carried the bitterness of Esau.
This is why Obadiah is not merely geopolitical.
It is deeply personal.
The prophecy burns because betrayal from enemies hurts.
But betrayal from family cuts differently.
God’s accusation against Edom was horrifying.
When Jerusalem fell...
Edom stood back and watched.
Worse than that.
They celebrated.
Obadiah 1:12 says:
“But do not gloat over your brother in the day of his misfortune.”
The Hebrew word for “gloat” is:
“תֵּרֶא” (tere’eh)
It carries the idea of looking upon with satisfaction. Watching with pleasure. Enjoying someone’s downfall.
That changes everything.
God was not only judging violence.
He was judging hearts that secretly enjoyed seeing others collapse.
That is terrifying.
Because some people never physically attack others.
They simply smile internally when someone fails.
A ministry falls. A marriage breaks. A believer backslides. Someone loses influence. Someone gets exposed. Someone struggles mentally. Someone sins publicly.
And hidden beneath religious language is a secret satisfaction:
“I knew they would fail.”
Obadiah reveals that heaven sees even silent cruelty.
The terrifying thing about Edom is they probably justified themselves.
They did not invade first. They did not light the fires. They only watched.
But God treated passive betrayal as active participation.
That should shake every modern believer.
Because neutrality during evil is not innocence.
The prophet describes Edom standing “at the crossroads” to cut off fugitives fleeing destruction.
Imagine the horror.
People escaping for their lives. Families running through smoke. Children terrified. Jerusalem burning.
And relatives blocked the escape routes.
How cold does a heart become before it can betray blood?
Yet humanity still does this.
People weaponize private pain. Expose vulnerable confessions. Exploit weakness. Use someone’s worst moment as entertainment.
Social media has normalized public executions of broken people.
And many believers participate while calling it discernment.
Obadiah stands like fire against that spirit.
The prophet’s message was not merely political judgment.
It was divine exposure.
God was exposing hidden pride.
Obadiah 1:3 says:
“The pride of your heart has deceived you.”
In Hebrew:
“זְדוֹן לִבְּךָ הִשִּׁיאֶךָ”
“zedon libbekha hishi’ekha”
“The arrogance of your heart has led you astray.”
Notice where the pride lived.
Not merely in behavior.
In the heart.
Pride is most dangerous when invisible.
Edom trusted its mountain fortresses. Its strategic defenses. Its elevated position. Its security. Its wisdom. Its alliances.
They believed they could not be touched.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals a terrifying pattern:
whatever people trust more than God eventually becomes the place of their humiliation.
For some it is beauty. For others money. Intelligence. Popularity. Influence. Followers. Control. Relationships. Ministry reputation.
Pride blinds people into believing they are untouchable.
Until God removes the illusion.
And here is where Obadiah becomes deeply uncomfortable.
Because Edom’s greatest sin was not only hatred.
It was distance.
Distance from compassion. Distance from mercy. Distance from grief. Distance from God’s heart.
People can become spiritually sophisticated while emotionally dead.
They know theology. Know verses. Know doctrine. Know apologetics. Know church culture.
Yet feel nothing when people break.
Obadiah destroys performative spirituality.
The prophet reminds us that God notices how people respond to another person’s suffering.
Not only their sermons. Not only their worship playlists. Not only their church attendance.
But their heart posture toward wounded people.
Jesus later echoed this same reality.
In Matthew 25, the Greek language becomes deeply piercing.
“ἐφ’ ὅσον οὐκ ἐποιήσατε”
“eph’ hoson ouk epoiēsate”
“As you did not do it...”
The judgment was connected not merely to evil committed.
But compassion withheld.
That is the terrifying bridge between Obadiah and Christ’s teachings.
Sin is not only what people do.
Sometimes it is what they refused to do.
Refused to say. Refused to help. Refused to heal. Refused to protect.
And somewhere reading this...
someone feels convicted.
Not because you attacked someone.
But because you watched them drown emotionally and justified your silence.
Obadiah reaches directly into modern hearts.
This tiny prophetic book is emotionally enormous.
And yet hidden inside the judgment is one of the greatest revelations of God’s justice.
Evil does not escape heaven’s attention.
People often wonder if God sees betrayal. If He notices manipulation. If He sees hidden cruelty. If He sees what people whispered behind closed doors. If He notices those who exploited weakness.
Obadiah answers clearly.
Yes.
God saw Edom.
Every smirk. Every celebration. Every moment of hidden satisfaction. Every blocked escape route. Every betrayal.
Nothing escaped Him.
That matters deeply for wounded believers.
Because many people carry pain from spiritual betrayal.
Friends who vanished during depression. Churches that abandoned them. Leaders who humiliated them. Family who mocked their faith. People who watched them suffer and offered no mercy.
Obadiah reminds the wounded:
God saw it.
And He still sees it.
But the book also warns the wounded not to become Edom themselves.
Pain can mutate into bitterness.
Victims can become cruel.
The rejected can become rejectors.
The betrayed can become betrayers.
The cycle continues unless grace interrupts it.
And that is where the Gospel enters this ancient prophetic fire.
Because Obadiah ultimately reveals humanity’s desperate need for a Savior.
Every person has traces of Edom hiding somewhere inside.
Jealousy. Hidden pride. Secret satisfaction at someone else’s failure. Emotional distance. Self-righteousness.
The human heart without Christ naturally drifts toward hardness.
This is why the Gospel is not motivational self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
The Greek word for repentance in the New Testament is:
“μετάνοια” (metanoia)
It means a transformative change of mind and heart.
Not superficial regret.
Transformation.
Jesus does not merely improve hard hearts.
He replaces them.
Ezekiel 36:26 prophetically declared:
“I will remove the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.”
Obadiah shows us the danger of stone hearts.
Jesus offers new ones.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Even proud people can repent. Even betrayers can be restored. Even spiritually cold hearts can become alive again.
Peter denied Christ. Yet became restored.
Paul persecuted believers. Yet became transformed.
The cross itself proves God specializes in redeeming broken people.
And maybe that is why Obadiah matters now more than ever.
Because modern culture rewards mockery. Rewards exposure. Rewards humiliation. Rewards public destruction.
But the Kingdom of God moves differently.
Mercy. Compassion. Restoration. Truth with tears. Correction with humility.
Not performative outrage.
Obadiah is a warning to every believer becoming emotionally numb.
The book asks uncomfortable questions:
Have you secretly enjoyed someone’s collapse?
Have you become prideful in your spiritual position?
Have you mistaken distance for wisdom?
Have you withheld compassion?
Have you watched people bleed emotionally while protecting your own comfort?
And perhaps hardest of all:
Have you become so wounded that you now resemble the very people who hurt you?
Those questions linger.
Because Scripture was never meant to merely inform minds.
It was meant to expose souls.
And still...
even after judgment...
God leaves room for hope.
The final verse of Obadiah says:
“And the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.”
In Hebrew:
“וְהָיְתָה לַיהוָה הַמְּלוּכָה”
“ve-hayetah l’YHWH ha-melukhah”
“The kingdom belongs to Yahweh.”
That is the ending humanity desperately needs.
Not Edom winning. Not pride winning. Not betrayal winning. Not cruelty winning.
God reigns.
And because He reigns, evil will not write the final chapter.
Jesus Christ already stepped into humanity’s violence, betrayal, mockery, and hatred.
He was betrayed by one of His own. Mocked publicly. Abandoned in suffering. Humiliated before crowds.
The Son of God understands betrayal personally.
Yet from the cross He still prayed:
“Father, forgive them.”
That changes everything.
Because forgiveness is not weakness.
It is proof heaven is stronger than hatred.
Maybe that is why this forgotten prophet still burns after thousands of years.
Obadiah is not merely ancient history.
It is a divine interruption.
A warning. A mirror. A confrontation. A mercy.
And maybe while reading this...
you realized the Holy Spirit exposed something hidden inside you.
Pride. Bitterness. Secret resentment. Spiritual arrogance. Compassion fatigue.
Do not run from conviction.
Conviction is often proof God still wants you.
The most dangerous heart is not the convicted heart.
It is the comfortable one.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this...
Not to shame them.
But because some people are silently becoming emotionally numb and do not even realize it.
One day many people will realize they were losing their soul long before they lost their reputation.
